breakouts.title: KOLUSU: Scariest South Indian Horror BGM (original score)
breakouts.summary: KOLUSU got 52 views against a usual 11.5 (about 4.5x). The likely reason is a clear horror topic posted two days before Halloween with a title people search for ("Scariest South Indian Horror BGM"), built on a local sound South Indian horror fans already know: kolusu anklet bells. The best evidence is RED LINE, posted in the same minute, which got 22 views. With 52 views and no Analytics data, this is a hint to test, not proof.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 52 against a channel median of about 11.5, so roughly 4.5x. It ranks 5th of 21 Shorts in this batch. Three Shorts did much better: "They exiled him 3 years ago" (559), THE RETURN (319) and NEON RAJA (245). KOLUSU is a mid-sized win, not the channel's best.
- **Likes per 100 views:** KOLUSU has 1 like, which is 1.9 per 100. The whole channel is at 2.4 per 100, but 28 of its 33 likes come from "exiled". Without that one Short the rest of the channel is at 0.6 per 100, so KOLUSU earned likes about 3x better than a typical BGM Short. With only one like, this could easily be chance.
- **Comments:** 0, the same as all 21 Shorts. Nobody is commenting yet on any Short.
- **Best comparison:** RED LINE (car chase BGM) went up at the same minute (29 Oct, 23:50 IST) and got 22 views. Same channel, same time, same title style, same tag. KOLUSU got 2.4x more, so the difference is most likely the topic and its keywords, not the publish time.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** Retention, traffic sources and countries are all empty. We can't tell whether people found it through the Shorts feed or through search, whether they watched to the jump scares, or whether the views came from India or from the US/UK around Halloween. At this size, 30 extra views can come from one recommendation test.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The team's own notes for the track (Kolusu v2) say the anklet bells were moved "up front" after v1 had no audible anklet. If the published cut opens on the bells, the first sound is a trigger South Indian viewers recognise from horror films: a ghost's chilanka or kolusu (anklet bells) walking through an empty house, a familiar trope in films like Chandramukhi. That sound tells viewers the genre in under a second, before any melody starts. Guess: this, plus the two jump scares the description promises, made people hold on past second 2 and wait for the scare.

## Psychology
- **Watch:** The title promises the "scariest" BGM. That is a dare, and people click to see if it lives up to it.
- **Finish:** The description promises two jump scares and a ghost "right behind you". Viewers who know a scare is coming stay for it (anticipation).
- **Loop:** Guess: if the Short ends on a scare, some people replay it to catch what they missed.
- **Like:** Horror is a strong feeling that is safe to have, and strong feelings get more likes than calm moods like GOLDEN HOUR (0 views).
- **Share:** "Headphones on, lights off" is the kind of dare people send to friends. It got no comments, which suggests the Short asks no question and gives viewers nothing to answer.

## Topic and timing
- **When:** It went up two days before Halloween (31 Oct), when Halloween horror-music playlists and "scary music" searches peak worldwide.
- **What:** Horror is a genre people search for by name, while a "romantic walk" or "cute dog" BGM is not.
- **Local angle:** Searches showed South Indian horror films and OTT horror releases around these dates. Guess: "South Indian horror" pulled Indian viewers and the Halloween season pulled US/UK viewers. The countries report needs to confirm this before we rely on it.
- **When it took off:** Unknown; there is no hourly data yet.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title pattern:** "NAME: Superlative + Region + Genre + BGM (original score)". It holds three words people search for (horror BGM, South Indian, scariest). Other titles in the same pattern with weaker search words got 0 to 16 views.
- **Description:** It opens with a second-person scene ("she is right behind you"), lists the sounds, then gives the dare. The hashtags #horrorbgm, #tamilhorror and #jumpscare match the search words.
- **Thumbnail:** Not known. Shorts feed views mostly see the first frame instead.

## Audience and algorithm
Guess: mostly the Shorts feed testing the video on fans of horror and BGM, plus a small amount of search for "horror bgm" and "tamil horror". Search would explain why it beat RED LINE, which went up at the same time. There is no sign of external traffic. The channel's real growth lane is still hero, villain and comeback stories (exiled, RETURN, NEON RAJA). KOLUSU shows that a second lane, folk horror timed to a season, can at least outdo its same-day siblings.

## What did not matter
- **Publish time:** RED LINE went up in the same minute and got 22.
- **"(original score)" and the AI disclosure:** Every Short has them, including the ones with 0 views.
- **Comments:** 0 everywhere.
- **Posting volume:** About 21 Shorts in 3 days did not stop KOLUSU from standing out.
- **Calm moods:** Romance, cute dog and sacrifice BGMs got 0 to 27 views.

## Repeat this
- Build each track on one named, instantly recognisable South Indian sound (kolusu, udukkai, temple bell, oppari wail) and play it in the first second.
- Pick a genre people search for (horror, villain entry, hero entry) and post it 48 to 72 hours before a date when demand peaks.
- Use the title pattern: superlative + region + genre + "BGM".
- Promise a payoff in the description (jump scare, drop) and add a dare (headphones on, lights off).

## Test next
- **Second horror Short:** Make another one built on a different folk sound, so we learn whether horror or the timing drove KOLUSU.
- **Ending:** Compare a version that ends on the jump scare and loops back to the bells with one that fades out.
- **Titles:** Test "Tamil horror BGM" against "South Indian horror BGM".
- **Comments:** Add a question that invites replies ("What time are you watching this?").
- **Analytics:** Check traffic sources and countries for KOLUSU, RED LINE and RETURN side by side.

- **Timing caveat:** I don't know when these view counts were taken. This Short went up at 17:00 IST, the earliest of the 10 uploads on 30 Oct. Four of those uploads have 0 views and were posted between 21:15 and 23:30, so some of this "breakout" is probably just having more hours online.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
No script came with the Short. The description suggests it opens on a black helicopter landing in snow. That is a strong opening image: big, dark and easy to read on a phone. My guess is that it does the same job as the exile Short's title: it shows an arrival before anything is explained. Most of the channel's low performers name a mood ("Romantic Walk", "Emotional Sacrifice") instead of opening on an event.

## Psychology
- **Payoff:** the feeling of a king coming back, with a whole valley lighting fires for him. This is the "mass" moment South Indian audiences replay and share.
- **Curiosity gap:** "an alternative theme" invites fans of Deepak Dev's real Khureshi theme to ask: is this as good as the original? That pulls them in to judge it (guess).
- **Familiar pattern:** the story already lives in viewers' heads, so they understand it with no voice-over.
- **Why no comments:** nothing in the video or text asked a question, so nobody had a reason to reply.

## Topic and timing
- **The subject:** Khureshi-Ab'raam is Mohanlal's character in Lucifer (2019) and L2: Empuraan (2025). Lucifer 3 is confirmed but has no date, so fan interest is always there.
- **That day:** on 30 Oct 2026 at 8:19 AM, Mohanlal posted "#L368" on X, which got about 44K views. I couldn't confirm what it announced. If it was a new film announcement, Malayalam fan activity was high that day (guess).
- **Coming up:** Kerala Piravi (Kerala's state day) is on 1 November, two days later. That is a good moment for Malayalam pride content.
- **Similar videos:** there are many "Khureshi Ab'raam Entry BGM" uploads from March 2025, which shows the name still gets searched.
- **Countries:** most likely India (Kerala) and the Gulf, but this is unconfirmed without analytics.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** it contains an exact name fans search for and says it is fan-made. It is long, and the "| Kingdom" ending adds nothing.
- **What didn't work elsewhere:** the channel's default format, "NAME: Mood BGM (original score)", mostly gets 0 to 30 views. The best title on the channel is a story sentence, not a label.
- **Description:** the "NOT Mohanlal" disclaimer protects the channel and should stay. The #Lalettan and #KhureshiAbraam hashtags connect it to the fandom.
- **Thumbnail:** it is unknown.

## Audience and algorithm
This is a guess until analytics arrive. The 59 views are probably a mix of a small Shorts-feed test plus search and suggested traffic from people who looked up Khureshi or Empuraan BGM. The 489-view exile Short shows that the Shorts feed can push this story further when people engage with it (28 likes). "THE RETURN" got 319 views but 0 likes. That looks like a feed test where viewers watched but didn't engage, so it stopped growing.

## What did not matter
- **"(original score)" in the title:** it appears on both winners and losers, so it doesn't explain the difference.
- **Genre labels:** cyberpunk, horror, car chase and romance all mostly got low numbers.
- **More uploads in one day:** posting 10 Shorts on 30 Oct didn't lift any single one of them.
- **Separate full-song uploads:** the Tamil song got 1 view.

## Repeat this
- Lead with an exiled or returning hero entry.
- Open on the arrival image.
- Name a famous mass character as "in the style of", with an original AI face and the disclaimer.
- Title it like a story sentence.
- Post it as the first upload of the day.

## Test next
- Put the same Kingdom cut out again under a story-sentence title ("Exiled 3 years. Tonight the valley burns for him") and compare it with the fandom-name title.
- Do a Kerala Piravi version on 1 November.
- Try "Rolex style" and "Dilli style" entries to see whether the boost comes from Khureshi specifically or from any fandom name.
- Measure every Short at 48 hours, so late uploads aren't unfairly judged.
- Get retention and traffic data for the next study.

breakouts.name: ÆTHER
breakouts.title: NEON RAJA: Cyberpunk King BGM (original score)
breakouts.summary: NEON RAJA got about 20 times the channel's usual views (266 against 13). Its publish time and its music were both tested elsewhere and didn't explain the jump. A Short at the same 19:00 slot got 12 views, and an earlier cut of the same track got 8. The likely cause, still a guess until the traffic data is checked, is the idea and how it was packaged: a named king, a mass hero-entry theme and an unusual mix of South Indian mass music with cyberpunk. That is the same hero-arrives-in-power idea behind the channel's other two hits, THE RETURN and 'They exiled him 3 years ago'.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
NEON RAJA has 266 views against a channel norm of 13, about 20 times usual. The other 18 Shorts in this batch have 1,067 views between them, and 74% of those come from just two videos: 'They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back.' (489) and THE RETURN: Hero Entry BGM (319). Most of the rest got between 0 and 39. So the channel doesn't grow steadily. It has occasional spikes, and all three spikes are about a hero arriving in power.

Likes per 100 views:
- NEON RAJA: 1.1 (3 likes)
- The other Shorts titled as a BGM: 0.5 (3 likes on 578 views)
- The exiled Short: 5.7, the best on the channel
- THE RETURN: 0 likes, even with 319 views

No Short on the channel has a single comment. So NEON RAJA reached people who liked it a little more than usual for a BGM title, but it did not excite them like the story-titled Short did.

Retention, traffic sources and countries are all empty. Because of that, the numbers can't yet tell us:
- whether people watched to the end or looped it
- whether the views came from the Shorts feed or from search
- which countries watched
- whether 266 is a real break-out or one round of YouTube testing the Short on new viewers that then stopped

The Shorts posted after 21:00 on 30 Oct have also had less time to collect views, so their zeros don't prove much.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script on file, so this part is partly a guess. The description promises 'a new sound taking the hook every few seconds' and a king's entry, so the opening probably gives a strong image (a ruler in neon rain) together with a hard musical hit. The best evidence is the Sport Cut of the same track (29 Oct, 8 views). Same music, a different opening and title, and roughly 30 times fewer views. Whatever NEON RAJA shows in its first frame and its title is likely what made the difference, not the track. Guess: the king's figure is visible right away, while the Sport Cut opened on action with no clear character.

## Psychology
The emotion behind it is hero elevation, the goosebumps moment from South Indian films when the hero walks in and the music swells. 'Raja' in a cyberpunk city also opens a curiosity gap: what does a mass hero entry sound like on synths? A familiar feeling in an unfamiliar setting makes people stop scrolling and keep watching. The likes show mild approval. The zero comments show there was no question, argument or invitation for viewers to respond to. The exiled Short shows what a story does: the line 'exiled... came back' gives a revenge payoff, and it earned 5 times the likes rate.

## Topic and timing
The topic sits where the channel's demand really is: hero, king and return themes. Publish time is ruled out because THE OATH went out at the same 19:00 IST slot and got 12. The date was a Friday evening in India, the eve of Halloween and nine days before Diwali (8 November 2026). I found no news event linked to it. Guess: Indian social media often features AI-made 'king' and cyberpunk-Indian visuals, and fans have recently debated an AI-made fake 'leaked scene' from Shah Rukh Khan's film King, so 'King' may be a word people already click on. I couldn't confirm this, so treat it as unproven. Countries are unknown, but the hashtags #tamilbgm and #massbgm point to India.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title 'NEON RAJA: Cyberpunk King BGM (original score)' names a character (Raja/King), a world (Cyberpunk/Neon) and a format (BGM). The Sport Cut said 'Cyberpunk Mass BGM', which has no character. DARK HORSE and CRIMSON VOWS also name only a role. The fan-made 'Khureshi-Ab'raam style entry' (59 views) shows that a known name helps too. The description is the same template as every other upload, so it didn't make the difference. The thumbnail is unknown, since Shorts in the feed mostly show the first frame.

## Audience and algorithm
It most likely reached people in the Shorts feed while YouTube was testing it on new viewers (a guess). 266 views with few likes looks like one round of testing that never got pushed further. Search is possible for 'hero bgm' and 'mass bgm'. THE RETURN's 319 views with 0 likes looks more like steady search traffic. External traffic is unlikely. The owner needs to check the traffic sources in YouTube Studio to settle this.

## What did not matter
- Publish time: same slot as THE OATH, which got 12
- The track itself: the Sport Cut got 8
- Hashtags and the AI disclosure: the same on every upload
- Emojis in titles
- Genre labels alone: 'Mass Hero Entry BGM' (DARK HORSE) got 0, though it is young

## Repeat this
A named hero or king plus a world that clashes with his style, opening on his entry with the hook in the first beat. Write the title as Name: Character + World + BGM. Keep the hero-elevation emotion, because all three spikes share it.

## Test next
1. A NEON RAJA Part 2 with the same character.
2. A story-sentence title against a 'Name: Character BGM' title on two hero-entry Shorts.
3. An opening shot that is the character's face against one that is the world.
4. A last frame that asks viewers to answer something, to get the first comments.

Comment 👑 and we'll make Part 2.' 3) Create a public playlist called 'Hero Entry & King BGMs' and add NEON RAJA, THE RETURN, the exiled Short and DARK HORSE.

Mr. Focus: Make at least half of each day's Shorts hero-arrival themes (king, return, exile, entry) where a named ruler or hero meets a world that clashes with his style, like cyberpunk Raja, desert Raja or space Raja.
Mr. Pen: Open every Short with the hero already in frame and the main musical hit landing at 0.0 seconds, with no build-up or establishing shot first.
Mr. Pen: End every hero-entry Short on a still frame with one on-screen question viewers can answer in a word (e.g. 'Who does Raja fight next?') to get comments.
Mr. Cut: Cut on the beat and change the shot each time a new instrument takes the hook (every 2-3 seconds), keeping the hero in at least every other shot.
Mr. Spark: Write titles as 'NAME: [Character noun such as King, Raja or Exiled Prince] + [World] BGM (original score)' and never use only a genre or role word like 'Mass' or 'Hero Entry' with no character.
Mr. Cast: Make Neon Raja a recurring character with the same look (neon crown, rain, city skyline) in every follow-up so viewers recognise him.
Mr. Hope: Publish NEON RAJA Part 2 within 7 days, and alongside it one hero-entry Short with a story-sentence title in the style of 'They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back.', then compare views and likes per 100 views after 48 hours.

breakouts.name: Sawaal
breakouts.title: 3 चुनाव आयुक्त, फ़ैसला किसका? सुप्रीम कोर्ट में SIR पर सवाल #Shorts
breakouts.summary: This Short got 94 views against a usual 28, but almost all of that lift came from the subject, not the video itself. Every Hindi Short this week about the Election Commission's special voter-roll revision (SIR) and the Supreme Court case did 3 to 17 times the channel's usual views, and this one was actually the weakest of them. It rode the news that broke on 26-27 October, when the Commission filed a 248-page affidavit and the court gave petitioners 10 days to reply. Its title asked a vague question, it covered an angle the channel had already posted, and it went up just 36 minutes after the channel's best Short, so it took in spillover views but held people less well.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
94 views is 3.3x the channel's usual 28.5. But look at the other Shorts and the picture changes. The five Hindi Shorts on the Election Commission (EC) and SIR story from 26-29 Oct got 101, 372, 484, 94 and 160 views. That is an average of 242 and a middle value of 160, so this Short came last in its own group. The four Hindi Shorts on other topics (BRICS 18, electoral bonds 14, women's reservation 21, voting at 18 24) averaged 19. The English versions got 33 and 0, against 101 and 14 for the same Shorts in Hindi.
Likes per 100 views: this Short 1.06, the rest of the channel 1.39 (17 likes on 1,227 views), and the best Short (the one about the PM removing the Chief Election Commissioner, or CEC) 2.27. Comments: 0, against 0.24 per 100 for the channel. So viewers reacted less than average. The views came from how YouTube spread it, not from people responding to it. YouTube Analytics came back empty: no retention, traffic sources or countries. We can't tell how far people watched, whether views came from the Shorts feed or search, or where viewers were. Every point about how it was distributed below is a **guess**.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
No script was provided. Going by the title, the hook was probably 'there are 3 commissioners, so whose decision is it?'. That is a puzzle with no clear answer and nothing at stake for the viewer. The 484-view Short opened with a yes/no question about a named office doing a specific thing ('Can the PM alone remove the CEC?'). The 372-view Short promised a concrete event (the EC's reply in court). **Guess:** the abstract opening is why this one held people less well than the others in its group.

## Psychology
What worked was a conflict over who holds power: petitioners say the CEC acted alone, while the EC's affidavit says all three commissioners agreed. Two official versions that contradict each other leave a gap people want to see closed. But the Short can't close it, because the court hasn't ruled, so viewers had nothing to like or argue about. The best Shorts either had a yes/no question with an answer the viewer could check, or touched the viewer's own vote ('3 crore voters cut?', Delhi's 33 lakh notices). This one had neither of those personal hooks.

## Topic and timing
The EC filed its affidavit on the night of 26 Oct, saying all SIR orders were unanimous and Form 6 (the voter-registration form) was not changed. On 27 Oct the Supreme Court gave petitioners 10 days to reply. A separate case challenging the CEC's powers had been running since the Indian Express report of 22 Sep. Delhi's SIR hearing was on 28 Oct and Delhi's claims window closed on 30 Oct. Reports put the next main hearing on 17 Nov, after Diwali (8 Nov). This Short went up at 03:06 IST on 28 Oct, about 28 hours after the news broke and 9 hours after the channel's own 372-view Short on the same affidavit. It was late and covered the same ground. Country data is missing. India is assumed.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title opens with a number ('3 चुनाव आयुक्त'), which matches the channel's better titles, but 'फ़ैसला किसका?' ('whose decision?') is vague. 'SIR' only comes at the end. The description is good: it gives both sides, names sources, discloses the AI and promises a follow-up. But descriptions rarely bring views on Shorts. The thumbnail was not provided.

## Audience and algorithm
**Guess:** this went up 36 minutes after the 484-view PM Short on the same topic. YouTube most likely showed it to the same viewers in the Shorts feed or next to that Short, as a follow-on. That would explain why it beat the channel's usual number but stayed far below its sibling. Search may have played a small part, since 'SIR' and 'Supreme Court' were trending terms (unconfirmed). There is no sign of outside traffic: no comments, one like.

## What did not matter
- **Publish hour:** Shorts at 08:00 got 160 and 24 views. Shorts in the small hours got 484 and 18. The topic decided the result, not the time.
- **Like/comment prompts and 'stay tuned' lines:** these brought no engagement.
- **Length and quality of the description:** the sources and AI disclosure are needed for trust but do not bring views.
- **English versions:** they consistently did worse.

## Repeat this
Stay on the live EC/SIR/Supreme Court story while it is in the news. Post within hours of each new court filing or order. Lead with a yes/no question about a named office and a specific power, or with a number that touches the viewer's own vote. Bring each Short something the channel hasn't already said.

## Test next
1. A yes/no title ('क्या CEC अकेले SIR आदेश दे सकते हैं?') against a 'whose?' title on the same news.
2. An angle about the viewer's own vote ('क्या आपका नाम कटा?' – 'Was your name cut?') against an angle about the institution.
3. Two same-story Shorts 4 or more hours apart against 30 minutes apart, so we can see whether they cannibalise each other. (This is a test of spacing, not a cut in output.)
4. A countdown Short before the 17 Nov hearing.
breakouts.owner: 1) Pin this comment under this Short and under the 484-view PM Short: 'सुप्रीम कोर्ट में SIR मामले की अगली सुनवाई दिवाली के बाद है। आप किस सवाल का जवाब सबसे पहले जानना चाहते हैं? नीचे लिखिए, हम अगली Short में पूछेंगे।' (Rough meaning: 'The next Supreme Court hearing on SIR is after Diwali. Which question do you most want answered first? Write it below and we will ask it in our next Short.') 2) Create a public playlist called 'SIR और सुप्रीम कोर्ट' ('SIR and the Supreme Court') with the 101, 372, 484, 94 and 160-view Shorts in date order, and add each new Short on this story to it. 3) Once a second outlet confirms the 17 November hearing date, replace 'दिवाली की छुट्टी के बाद' ('after the Diwali break') in this description with the exact date. 4) Check that YouTube Analytics access is working so that retention, traffic sources and countries come through for the next study.
breakouts.changes:
Mr. Focus: Until the Supreme Court's 17 Nov SIR hearing is over, pick at least half of each day's Shorts from the live Election Commission/SIR/CEC-powers story, and make sure each one brings a new fact, filing or number the channel has not already covered.
Mr. Pen: Make the first spoken line a yes/no question naming one specific office or body and one concrete power or number (for example, 'क्या CEC अकेले SIR आदेश दे सकते हैं?'), never an open 'whose/what/how' question, and answer it from the sourced document within the next two lines.
Mr. Spark: Write Hindi titles as a yes/no question or a number-plus-claim, with 'SIR', 'चुनाव आयोग' or 'CEC' in the first 30 characters and at least one figure (voters, notices, pages, days), keeping them under 60 characters before #Shorts.
Mr. Cut: In the first 2 seconds, show the key number or document (for example '248 पन्ने', '3 करोड़') as large on-screen Hindi text over a real Wikimedia photo of the institution, with no title card or logo before it.
Mr. Cast: Have one anchor ask the viewer's yes/no question and the other answer it by naming the source on air (for example 'हलफ़नामे के मुताबिक़' – 'according to the affidavit'), so the two sides of every dispute are always given to different speakers and neither anchor offers an opinion.
Mr. Hope: When two Shorts on the same story are ready on the same day, publish the yes/no or personal-vote angle first and the institutional angle at least 4 hours later, and judge each Short against the average for its topic group rather than the overall channel average.

breakouts.name: Kissa
breakouts.title: Ep 15 | 100 दिन का रिश्ता: घर के अंदर का फ़ोन, बंद कमरा और दूसरी चाबी
breakouts.summary: Ep 15 got 50 views, about 6-7x the channel's median of 7.5 across 14 comparable Shorts, and it was the only recent episode to get likes (3, or 6 per 100 views). Ep 16, posted 11 minutes later, did even better with 78 views, so most of the jump probably came from the time slot. Both went out at 07:30 IST after a 30-hour break, instead of in the late-night or 7-minute-apart dumps that held other episodes to 0-23 views. On top of that, Ep 15 had the series' clearest single hook: a phone ringing inside the house, a room locked for 20 years, and a second key that points at the husband.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** Ep 15 has 50 views. The other 14 earlier episodes have a median of 7.5 and a mean of 10.4, so this is about 6-7x usual. It is also the second-newest Short, so it has had the least time to collect views.
- **The main confound:** Ep 16 went up 11 minutes later and has 78 views. The breakout belongs to the **morning of 28 Oct as a slot**, not to Ep 15 alone.
- **Likes per 100 views:** Ep 15 got 3 likes, which is 6.0 per 100. Every other Short together has 2 likes on 224 views, about 0.9 per 100. Ep 16 has 0 likes on 78 views. So Ep 15 got the strongest reaction from the people who saw it, while Ep 16 got the most reach.
- **Comments:** 0 everywhere, so the channel has no comment signal at all.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** The analytics export came back empty: no retention, no traffic sources, no countries. We cannot tell whether views came from the Shorts feed, the channel page or binge-watchers coming from Ep 16. We also don't know the snapshot time, and at 50 views one viewer who watched the whole series could move everything. Treat every cause below as a likely explanation, not a proven one.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
- **Second 0:** A whispered line to the thief: 'अगर डायरी तुम्हारे पास है... तो फ़ोन उठाओ।' It sets up a threat and a mystery before any backstory.
- **Seconds 1-2:** The buzzing comes from inside the house. 'The call is coming from inside the house' is one of the oldest and best-tested horror and mystery hooks, and it needs no knowledge of Ep 1-14.
- **Compared with Ep 9-13:** Those openers relied on series memory: Vikram, Banganga, Kavita, nurse Sharda, Aarav. Ep 15 is easy to follow on its own: one corridor, one door, one glowing phone. *Guess:* this is why it held new feed viewers better than its siblings.

## Psychology
- **Watching:** An open question (who is calling?) gets answered fast with a worse question: the phone shows Riya's own number, so the person is in this house.
- **Finishing:** Three short tightening steps: Dadi catches Riya, Kabir also missed dinner, and only Kabir has the second key. Each one raises the stakes in a few seconds.
- **Liking:** The episode doubles the cliffhanger. A taunting message ('भरोसा अब भी है, बहू?') arrives just as Kabir spots the hidden phone. Viewers carry two unresolved worries, and the like is the low-effort way to say 'I'm hooked'.
- **Commenting:** No one commented, even though 'is Kabir the thief?' is an obvious invitation to argue. Nobody asked the viewer to answer.
- **Emotions at work:** Suspicion of a trusted partner, and fear of being caught by an elder. In Indian family drama the bahu sneaking around while Dadi watches is instantly readable.

## Topic and timing
- **Genre heat:** Contract-marriage microdramas are hot right now. Adgully ran a piece on 27 Oct 2026, the day before publish, about Kuku TV microdramas built on contract marriages and family secrets. YouTube has also launched Shorts Series (seasons and episodes) for microdramas, which it says passed 6.5 billion views.
- **No outside event:** My search found no viral moment or holiday on 28 Oct tied to this subject. Diwali falls in early November, and *guess*, festive-season family drama may be getting extra viewing.
- **The slot is the strongest explanation:**
  - Ep 15 and 16 came out at 07:33 and 07:44 IST, after a gap of almost 30 hours.
  - On 26 Oct, Ep 5-9 went up 7-8 minutes apart and got 6, 2, 0, 9 and 8 views. Those Shorts were competing with each other.
  - Ep 12-14 went up between midnight and 2 AM IST and got 23, 2 and 14 views.
  - A morning commute slot after a pause looks like what got the feed to test the channel again.
- **Countries:** Unknown, since the analytics are empty.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** Three concrete objects in one line: फ़ोन, बंद कमरा, दूसरी चाबी. Ep 9-13 titles leaned on character names a newcomer can't place. Objects make a mystery a stranger can picture. *Guess:* this helped click-through and swipe-stay.
- **Description:** It gives away the 'inside the house' reveal but keeps the key-holder hidden. That is fine, because it gives away the setup and keeps the answer.
- **Hashtags:** Identical across all episodes, so they explain nothing.
- **Thumbnail:** We have no data on it, and Shorts mostly serve the first frame anyway.

## Audience and algorithm
- **Most likely:** The Shorts feed tested the morning pair on a small Hindi-speaking group. Ep 16 got wider distribution, and some Ep 16 viewers may have gone back to Ep 15. Ep 15's like rate fits a smaller but more engaged group.
- **Ruled out:** Search is unlikely for brand-new titles. External sharing is unlikely with 0 comments.
- **Unknown:** Retention and swipe-away rate are the missing proof.

## What did not matter
- Hashtags, the 'Ep N' prefix and the K-drama label were the same on every Short.
- Episode order: Ep 1 has 2 views, so viewers are not starting at the beginning.
- Comments: zero across the channel.
- Publishing more on one day: 10 episodes on 26 Oct averaged about 10 views each.

## Repeat this
- Publish the day's new episodes as a pair at 07:00-08:00 IST, not in midnight or minutes-apart bursts.
- Open on a sound or object inside the house in the first line, playable with zero backstory.
- Build each episode in one location with one secret object and one accusation of a trusted character.
- End on a double cliffhanger: a new message plus a direct question to the heroine.
- Title with 3 concrete objects or places, not new names.

## Test next
- 07:30 IST vs 19:30 IST pairs over a week.
- Object titles vs name titles on alternate episodes.
- An on-screen last-frame question ('कबीर या दादी?') to unlock comments.
- A Shorts Series playlist, to see whether old episodes get pulled up by new ones.

Pin a matching 'whom do you suspect' question under Ep 16. 2) In YouTube Studio, put Ep 1-16 into a Shorts Series / season playlist called '100 दिन का रिश्ता – सीज़न 1', and set Ep 16 as the related video on Ep 15 (and each episode's next one going forward). 3) Set the default scheduled publish time to 07:30 IST.

breakouts.name: ÆTHER
breakouts.title: THE RETURN: Hero Entry BGM (original score)
breakouts.summary: THE RETURN got 282 views on a channel where most Shorts get about 1. The likeliest reason is its subject: a hero coming home. Its sister upload with the same theme, 'They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back.', did even better (389 views, 23 likes), and together the two 'return' Shorts got about 96% of the channel's views that night. Being among the first uploads of a 12-Short batch probably helped YouTube test it. The 0 likes suggest the BGM-style title drew passive viewers, while the story-style title earned real emotional engagement.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Size of the breakout:** 282 views against a channel median of about 1. The other 11 Shorts got 389, 7, 6, 5, 3, 1 and five zeros.
- **It wasn't the top Short that night.** The sister upload "They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back." (21:01 IST, 49 minutes earlier) got 389 views. The two 'return' Shorts got 671 of the 698 views that batch earned (about 96%).
- **Likes and comments per 100 views:**
  - THE RETURN: 0 likes, 0 comments.
  - The exile Short: 5.9 likes per 100.
  - The other ten Shorts: 1 like on 22 views.
  - So THE RETURN got the reach but none of the emotional response.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics is empty (no retention, traffic sources or countries). We can't say whether viewers stayed past the drop, whether the views came from the Shorts feed, hashtag pages or search, or whether India led. The 0 likes on 282 views could mean early swipe-aways or quiet listeners. Retention would tell us which. Pull 48-hour analytics before trusting any guess below.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
There is no script on file. The description promises "a quiet opening, then the return, then everything at once." Guess: a quiet opening risks swipes in the first second. That fits 282 views with zero likes: the feed served it, but few people stayed for the payoff. The exile Short's title gives the stakes before the first frame (exiled, 3 years, came back), so the quiet start feels like tension, not dead air. Next time, the stakes need to be on screen in second 0, and the hero needs to appear by about 2 seconds.

## Psychology
The emotion is the **homecoming / comeback**: the person who was wronged returns stronger. It is one of the most shared feelings in Indian mass cinema (the elevation scene). It is also a familiar, safe kind of goosebumps that people replay.
- The exile title opens a curiosity gap (why was he exiled, what will he do now?) and a sense of justice. That earns likes.
- "Hero Entry BGM" just names a genre. It brings in people browsing for music, who listen but rarely like or comment.
- Guess: a 'return' story pays off emotionally, while a 'BGM' label invites passive listening.
- Comments were 0 everywhere. Nothing in the video or description asks viewers anything.

## Topic and timing
- Published 29 Oct 2026, about 10 days before Diwali (8 Nov 2026). Diwali celebrates a hero's homecoming: Rama's return to Ayodhya.
- Guess: the homecoming theme may have fit a festive mood, especially in India. There is no country data to confirm this.
- web_search found no specific viral moment, film release or 'hero entry' trend that day.
- Hero-entry BGM is a steady evergreen search category in South Indian film music (Thaman- and Anirudh-style ringtones). It is a good long-term lane, not a one-day spike.
- When it took off and from where is unknown until Analytics fills in.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** the strongest clue is comparing titles line by line.
  - Every 'NAME: Genre BGM (original score)' title got 0 to 7 views, except THE RETURN.
  - The one plain story sentence got the most views and all the real likes.
  - THE RETURN probably beat the other BGM titles because of its topic, not its format.
- **Description:** solid. It includes a mood promise, "Headphones on, volume up," and good hashtags (#heroentrybgm #massbgm #elevationbgm). Guess: the hashtags may have brought some views from hashtag pages.
- **Thumbnail:** Shorts mostly ignore custom thumbnails. It didn't matter here.

## Audience and algorithm
Guess, with no traffic data: almost all views came from the Shorts feed test pool.
- On a new channel, the first uploads of a session got that test. The 21:01 and 21:50 Shorts were the two earliest, and both broke out.
- The Shorts uploaded from 22:41 onward got 0 to 7 views. That fits either the batch theory or the theme theory. Both 'return' Shorts being early makes it impossible to separate the two.
- The two near-duplicate pairs (MONSOON DUEL ×2, NEON RAJA ×2) each got 0 views. Posting two cuts of the same film did not double the chances.

## What did not matter
- **Genre range:** horror, car chase, cute dog, cyberpunk, sword fight and villain entry all got 0 to 7 views.
- **The '(original score)' tag:** it was on every title, both the ones that worked and the ones that didn't.
- **Alternate cuts of one film** (Sport Cut, a second title).
- **A villain as the lead:** CRIMSON VOWS and the villain wedding Short got 6 and 3 views.
- **Late-night slots:** 23:00 to 00:50 IST got almost nothing.

## Repeat this
1. Make comeback / homecoming / exile-return hero stories the core lane.
2. Title with a story sentence that holds stakes and a time gap, then add the BGM tag.
3. Put the stakes on screen in the first second, the hero by about 2 seconds, then the drop.
4. Upload the strongest hero-return concept first in every batch, around 21:00 IST.
5. Keep the hero-entry hashtag set.

## Test next
- **Title format:** the same film with 'Story sentence | Hero Entry BGM' vs 'NAME: Hero Entry BGM'. Measure views and likes per 100 views.
- **Diwali homecoming:** a 'He came home for Diwali' return Short before 6 Nov, to see whether festival timing boosts the theme.
- **Opening:** a cold open that starts at the drop vs a quiet build, compared on retention.
- **Comments:** a question in the last frame or the description ("Whose entry should he face next?") to break 0 comments.
- **Batch order:** a non-hero Short in the first slot, to tell the early-batch effect apart from the theme effect.

Who should he face next: the brother who betrayed him, or the king who exiled him? 👇'. Also open YouTube Studio for both Shorts and record retention, traffic sources and countries after 48 hours, because that data is missing from this study.

Mr. Focus: Make at least half of each batch comeback/homecoming hero stories (exiled, betrayed or presumed dead, then returns), and include one Diwali-homecoming return story to publish before 6 November.

Mr. Cut: Show the hero, a silhouette or a key object on screen within 2 seconds, and land the first big beat drop no later than second 3. Never open with more than 1 second of quiet.
Mr. Spark: Write titles as a short story sentence with stakes, then a separator and the BGM tag (e.g. 'They betrayed him at the altar. He came back. | Hero Entry BGM'), and keep #heroentrybgm #massbgm #elevationbgm in every hero description.

Mr. Hope: Upload the strongest hero-return Short first in every batch at about 21:00 IST, never post two cuts of the same film in one batch, and log 48-hour retention, traffic source, country and likes per 100 views for every Short.

breakouts.name: ÆTHER
breakouts.title: They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back.
breakouts.summary: This Short got 137 views when every other Short on the channel got 0 to 12. The likeliest reason is how it was framed: the title tells a story about a character (an exiled stallion coming home) instead of labelling a music genre. The clearest proof is that the same track, uploaded 49 minutes later as "THE RETURN: Hero Entry BGM", got only 12 views. Being the first upload of a 12-Short batch probably helped too (a guess), and the like rate of about 8 per 100 views suggests the people who saw it enjoyed it.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 137. The other 11 Shorts in the same three-hour batch got 16 views between them (12, 3, 1 and eight zeros). Since the usual is 0, the honest comparison is roughly 11x the next-best Short and about 8.5x everything else combined.
- **Likes:** 11, which is 8.0 per 100 views. The rest of the channel has 0 likes from 16 views, so the channel has no baseline to compare against. 8% is high for Shorts; a rough rule of thumb is 3–5% (guess-level benchmark).
- **Comments:** 0, the same as the rest of the channel.
- **Cleanest test:** "THE RETURN: Hero Entry BGM (original score)" uses the same track as this Short, published 49 minutes later, and got 12 views. Same music, different framing, about 11x the views. We don't know whether the visuals were identical.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics came back empty (no retention, no traffic sources, no countries). So we can't confirm whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, what share of viewers swiped away, or where viewers live. 137 views is also a small sample: this looks like YouTube's first test audience reacting well, not a true viral run. Everything below about why people watched is inferred from the titles, description and comparisons.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The script was not provided, so this part is a guess based on the description. The setup (a black stallion back on the mountain, a young king who has to answer) suggests the opening shows one powerful animal on a ridge, facing a herd. That image explains itself instantly, needs no voice-over, and works in any language, which fits a channel without narration. The BGM-labelled Shorts more likely open on atmosphere with no clear character or conflict. **Guess:** the stallion appears and the stakes are clear before the first beat drop.

## Psychology
- **Curiosity gap:** "They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back." raises two questions at once: why was he exiled, and what will he do now? People finish to see the confrontation.
- **Revenge or return arc:** the outcast-returns story is one of the oldest crowd-pleasers, and it matches the channel's "hero entry / mass BGM" audience exactly.
- **Likes:** the 8% like rate suggests the payoff delivered. The swelling score at the moment of return probably felt like a reward (guess).
- **Comments:** zero comments means nothing invited a reply. The ending likely resolved the story, or nobody asked viewers a question.
- **Animals:** animal stories travel across cultures without translation, so they suit a global, no-voice-over channel.

## Topic and timing
Web searches for 29 October 2026 found no news, trend or holiday linked to horses, exile stories or epic music. India's news that day was dominated by Cyclone Arnab, which has no link. **Timing is unlikely to explain it.** It was published at 21:01 IST (15:31 UTC, 11:31 US Eastern), during India's evening and the US late morning. It was also the **first of 12 uploads** in about three hours. **Guess:** the later uploads competed with each other for YouTube's limited test views on a tiny channel, and the first one got the cleanest test. No country data is available.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** the title is the biggest difference. The breakout title is a two-sentence story with a past wrong and a present turn, and no genre words. Nine of the other ten titles follow the pattern "NAME: Genre BGM (original score)". That pattern reads like a music catalogue entry, which most Shorts-feed viewers aren't looking for.
- **Description:** it continues the story first and only then credits the music, then adds hashtags.
- **The other story title:** "The villain came to his own wedding in style." also uses a story frame but got only 3 views. So a story title alone isn't enough. That one has no stakes, no time gap, no animal and no open question.
- **Thumbnail:** the thumbnail barely matters, because the Shorts feed autoplays instead of showing it.

## Audience and algorithm
This is a guess, since the traffic data is empty. At 137 views on a channel with no audience, almost all views probably came from the Shorts feed test pool, not from search (nobody searches that title) or external links. The 8% like rate is the kind of signal that earns a second, larger test batch. Whether that happens depends on retention, which we can't see yet.

## What did not matter
- **Music on its own:** the same track got 12 views when presented as BGM.
- **The hashtags:** they were the same across Shorts.
- **The AI disclosure:** it appears on every Short.
- **The genre:** the horror, chase, cyberpunk and sword-fight BGM Shorts all got 0, so no genre label helped.
- **Publishing a lot:** volume didn't lift any individual Short.

## Repeat this
1. Title every Short as a story: a wrong in the past, a turn in the present, and no "BGM" in the title.
2. Lead with one character, ideally an animal, whose stakes are clear in the first frame.
3. Time the character's big moment to the score's drop.
4. Put the story-cut version of each track first in the batch, and the BGM-labelled version later.

## Test next
- A Part 2 with the same black stallion, to see whether a returning character keeps the lift.
- The same exile-and-return arc with a different animal (wolf, elephant, eagle), to see whether it's the arc or the horse.
- An ending that leaves the confrontation unresolved, to try to get comments.
- Two story titles on the same film, one with a time gap and one without, to find out whether "3 years ago" matters.

Mr. Spark: Write every Short title as a two-part story in plain words: a past wrong, then a present turn (for example "They exiled him 3 years ago. Today he came back."). Keep it under 55 characters, never put "BGM" or "(original score)" in the title, and credit the track in the description's second paragraph.
Mr. Focus: Base each Short on one clear story arc (exile and return, underdog revenge, an outcast taking the throne), and prefer a single animal or creature hero whose stakes are clear without words.
Mr. Pen: In the first 2 seconds, show the hero already arriving (a silhouette on a ridge or at a gate) and put on-screen text of 8 words or fewer stating the past wrong. Save the confrontation for the beat drop.
Mr. Cut: Reveal the hero's face or full body exactly on the score's first major drop, cut on the beat after that, and end on a frame that loops back into the opening shot.
Mr. Cast: Make the black stallion a recurring hero with the same look (black coat, scar or mane detail) in every chapter, and give each rival a distinct look.
Mr. Hope: In every batch, publish the story-titled cut of each track first, publish the BGM-labelled version of the same track afterward, and log views and likes per 100 views for both.
Mr. Pen: End every story Short on an open question, either unresolved on screen or asked in the closing text (for example "Throne or exile?"), so viewers have a reason to comment.

breakouts.name: Sawaal
breakouts.title: दिल्ली SIR: 33 लाख नोटिस, 1.87 लाख मामले अटके! #Shorts
breakouts.summary: This Short got 109 views against a usual 33, about 3.3 times normal. Most likely it took off because it was about the hottest story the channel covers, the Delhi voter-roll revision (SIR) and the Election Commission, and it went out at 08:00 IST on 29 October, one day before the 30 October deadline for claims and objections. It also led with big, official, local numbers that tell a Delhi viewer to check their own name. Another Short posted at exactly the same minute got only 12 views, so the posting time did not cause this. The topic, the deadline and the personal stake did.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 109 against a usual 33, about 3.3 times normal. It was the 3rd-best of the 10 Shorts in the list. The two above it are also Election Commission and Supreme Court stories: 'Can the PM alone remove the Chief Election Commissioner?' got 443 and 'EC's reply in the Supreme Court: 3 SIR orders and Form 6' got 372. So this is part of a hot topic group, not a one-off.
- **Likes:** 2 per 109 views, 1.8 per 100. The channel's other 9 Shorts together have 15 likes on 1,060 views, 1.4 per 100. That is slightly better than usual, but with only 2 likes it could be chance.
- **Comments:** 0. The other Shorts average 0.28 per 100 views. Nobody felt pushed to reply.
- **Retention, traffic sources and countries:** the YouTube Analytics fields arrived empty. So we cannot yet say how much of the video people watched, how many swiped away, whether views came from the Shorts feed or search, or which countries they came from.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** at roughly 100 views, a single share to one WhatsApp group could explain the whole jump (a guess). Treat every conclusion below as a direction to test, not proof.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The script was not provided, so the hook is inferred from the title and description (a guess). The likely opening is the place, the topic word and a huge official number: Delhi SIR, 33 lakh notices. A number that size instantly signals 'this could include me' to anyone living in Delhi. The best comparison is '18 के होते ही वोटER? अब साल में 4 मौके!' ('Voter at 18? Now 4 chances a year'), posted the same minute, which got 12 views. Its hook is an old rule (four qualifying dates a year have existed since 2022) with no deadline and a narrow audience (people about to turn 18).

## Psychology
- **Fear of loss plus personal stake:** 'मामले अटके' ('cases stuck') together with 33 lakh notices raises the question 'is my name, or my family's, at risk?' (a guess).
- **Deadline urgency:** the claims period ended the next day, and the description says 'अपना नाम अभी देख लें' ('check your name now'). Useful, urgent information is the kind people forward to family.
- **Why the open questions didn't matter here:** this Short gives an answer and a task, not an argument. That probably explains the zero comments: nothing to debate. The 443-view CEC Short, which asked a constitutional question, did get likes and a comment.

## Topic and timing
- **Why SIR:** SIR is the biggest live election story. In the same week, the Supreme Court heard a plea on 28 October asking the Election Commission to publish the list of voters who got notices (ETV Bharat). The Election Commission told the Court its three SIR orders were unanimous (Deccan Herald). On 29 October, CEO Delhi data showed 47.56 lakh names dropped from the draft roll and only 2.71 lakh new Form 6 applications (The Patriot, Deccan Chronicle).
- **Why this moment:** the Tribune's '94.34% notices disposed of, 3 days left' report came out on 27 October. The Short arrived at 08:00 IST on 29 October, when 'Delhi SIR last date' searches were probably peaking (a guess).
- **When it took off and where:** without analytics we can't see the day-by-day curve or the countries. Because it is in Hindi and about Delhi, it is most likely Delhi/NCR and north India (a guess).
- **Other channels:** I could not check how similar Shorts did on other channels because the web-search limit was reached. That is still an open gap.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** it puts the search keyword first ('दिल्ली SIR:'), then two hard numbers, then a status word with '!'. Every title in the top group names a specific institution or process (SIR, EC, Supreme Court, CEC). The weak ones are abstract (BRICS spending, 'one verdict', '4 chances').
- **Description:** it gives exact figures (31,26,576 notices, 94.34%), dates (30 Nov, 4 Dec), two sources and a clear action. That builds trust and probably helps search.
- **Thumbnail:** custom thumbnails play little part in the Shorts feed. Unknown here.
- **Language:** the English versions got 33 and 0 views. Hindi wins.

## Audience and algorithm
The sources are unknown. Best guess: a small Shorts-feed test (around 30 views, the channel's normal) worked well enough to unlock a second batch of viewers. Search for 'Delhi SIR' around the deadline probably added a share. Possibly one outside share as well.

## What did not matter
- **Publish time:** the same 08:00 slot gave 109 and 12.
- **AI anchors and visual style:** the same on every Short.
- **Hashtags:** a similar set on the flops.
- **Question-mark titles:** they appear on both winners and losers.
- **English versions:** they added nothing.

## Repeat this
- Cover SIR, Election Commission and Supreme Court stories that have a dated deadline or hearing within 72 hours.
- Lead with the place and the largest official number.
- Close with a concrete action and date ('check your name by…').
- Keep the double-sourced exact figures in the description.
- Follow the dates already announced: claims to be decided by 30 November, final roll on 4 December.

## Test next
1. Open with a 'you' line ('क्या आपका नाम सूची में है?', 'Is your name on the list?') versus opening with the number, on two SIR stories.
2. Run the same title formula for other states' SIR figures to see if the Delhi effect carries over.
3. End with a question that invites experiences ('आपके इलाके में BLO आए?', 'Did a BLO visit your area?') to lift comments while staying neutral.
4. Once analytics work, check whether search or the Shorts feed drives the deadline Shorts.

breakouts.name: Instinct
breakouts.title: 47 corneilles sur 53 : le masque qui les fait crier #Shorts
breakouts.summary: The crow-mask Short got 3.8× the channel's usual views (758 against 198). The most likely reasons are its topic and its hook. Corvid and bird Shorts are this channel's most reliable performers, and the opening says an animal took a grudge against a human, with a clear number (47 out of 53) and a mask on screen two days before Halloween. Retention, traffic and country data were empty, and its like rate was below the channel's. So the boost probably came from YouTube showing it to more people in the Shorts feed, not from viewers loving it unusually much. That part is a guess until Analytics arrives.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 758 against a usual 198, so **3.8×** the norm. That is real, but modest for this channel: it ranks 5th of the 15 recent Shorts. The stork story (1,596), the wire-hook crow (1,233) and the dolphin (1,192) all did better, and the parrot (778) roughly tied it.
- **The channel is split in two.** Shorts land either in the hundreds or under 20 views. So the useful question is what puts a Short in the upper group, not only what made this one special.
- **Likes:** 22 likes is **2.9 per 100 views**. The channel's other Shorts average **3.8 per 100** (238 likes on 6,302 views), and the dolphin (4.3), the wire-hook crow (4.1) and the 235 ms crow (3.9) did better. The mask Short reached more people than it pleased.
- **Comments:** 0, even with a direct question at the end. The whole channel has 2 comments in total.
- **Bird Shorts vs the rest:** among Shorts old enough to judge, the 5 bird Shorts average about **985 views**. The 8 non-bird Shorts average about **267**, and only the dolphin topped 1,000.
- **What the numbers can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics was empty, so there is no retention, swipe-away rate, traffic source or country data. Without them I can't confirm whether the hook held viewers or how far they watched into the caveat. The two Shorts from 29 Oct at 16:41 and 16:52 IST show 0 views, which probably just means they had not been out long enough. Leave them out of any comparison for now.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first spoken line is « 47 corneilles sur 53 ont crié sur cet homme… à cause de son masque. » The first image shows crows diving at a masked man, with 47/53 on screen. In two seconds that gives a precise number, a threat aimed at a person, and an unexplained cause (why the mask?). The bee Short went out at the same minute and also opened with a number (« 1 abeille, 1 zéro »), but it got half the views. The difference is probably not the number. It is that the crow hook puts a **human target** in the scene (*guess*). The stork story (a man saves a stork) and the parrot follow the same animal-and-human pattern.

## Psychology
- **Being judged by an animal.** The idea that crows remember your face and turn against you is a mild, enjoyable fear. It makes a viewer think about the crows they see every day.
- **Curiosity gap.** The hook says the crows reacted, but not why other crows that were never captured also reacted. That holds viewers until the turn: « la plupart n'avaient jamais été capturées ».
- **Family story.** Crows teaching their young to distrust a man is easy to retell, which probably helps sharing (*guess*).
- **Weak spots.** The ending question, « quel visage n'avez-vous jamais oublié ? », is personal and abstract and got 0 replies. The low like rate *may* mean the caveat-heavy second half (17 years, PET imaging, the reaction fading) took away some of the payoff (*guess*).

## Topic and timing
- **Publish time:** 05:00 Paris on Thursday 29 October 2026, two days before Halloween. France's Toussaint school holidays ran 17 October to 2 November, so families were at home with phones.
- **Season:** masks and crows both belong to the Halloween and Toussaint season. It is likely, but unproven, that the Shorts feed favoured a mask-and-crow video that week (*guess*). La Presse covered this same study around Toussaint in 2024, which suggests the story suits the season.
- **Evergreen subject:** in English it keeps resurfacing. ScienceBlog ran it twice in September 2026, and NOVA PBS on TikTok and several YouTube explainers have covered it. That shows audience demand. French Shorts on it seem rarer (*guess*).
- **Slot:** 05:00 Paris is morning in Europe and francophone Africa but midnight in Quebec. Without country data I can't say where the views came from.
- **No news hook:** I found no news event that day about crows or the study. The rise looks seasonal and topic-driven, not news-driven.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- **Title:** concrete and visual (masque, crier). But every Short on the channel uses the number-first format, flops included, so the format alone doesn't explain the result.
- **Description:** accurate, sourced and transparent about AI images. That builds trust but probably doesn't change reach.
- **Thumbnail:** rarely seen in the Shorts feed, so it probably had little effect.

## Audience and algorithm
The channel has very few subscribers and gets almost no comments, so the 758 views almost certainly came from the **Shorts feed**, not from search or outside links (*guess until traffic data arrives*). The pattern looks like this: YouTube tests each Short on a small group. Bird and animal-meets-human Shorts pass that test, and great-ape, elephant and dog Shorts stall below 20 views. The below-average like rate suggests YouTube stopped widening the audience at around 750 views.

## What did not matter
- **The 05:00 slot:** the dog Short at the same time got 17 views.
- **The number-first title format:** the flops use it too.
- **#Shorts and the hashtags.**
- **The comment question:** 0 replies.
- **The AI-image disclaimers:** no visible cost.
- **Narrator-only voice:** both hits and flops use it.

## Repeat this
- Birds, and corvids above all.
- An animal that **reacts to, remembers or judges a human**, shown in the first image.
- One clean ratio with a twist (animals that never saw it still learned it).
- Topics that fit the calendar, published a few days before the date.

## Test next
1. **Shorter script:** 40 s vs 55 s on the same kind of corvid story, comparing like rate and completion.
2. **Ending question:** a yes/no question about the viewer's own experience vs an open personal question, measured by comments.
3. **Slot for Quebec:** a 14:00 Paris slot vs 05:00 for the same topic type, checked with the country data.
4. **Retention:** pull this Short's retention and traffic data at day 7 and confirm or drop the guesses above.

breakouts.name: Kissa
breakouts.title: Ep 16 | 100 दिन का रिश्ता: साठवें दिन की धमकी, रिया का सच और कबीर का साथ
breakouts.summary: Ep 16 got 50 views against the channel's usual 7. The most likely reason is when it went out, not anything special about the episode. It and Ep 15 were posted together on a weekday morning (07:33 and 07:44 IST) after a 30-hour gap. Every earlier episode went out in batches minutes apart, or after midnight. The script probably helped too: it opens with an accusation and ends by turning suspicion on the hero. But at 50 views, with no Analytics data and 0 likes, this is a weak signal, not proof.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** Ep 16 got 50 views. The median of the other 15 Shorts is 7, so it did about 7x the usual. Ep 15, posted 11 minutes earlier, got 42. Together the two make up 92 of the channel's 217 total views (42%).
- **Likes and comments per 100 views:** Ep 16 has 0 likes and 0 comments. Ep 15 has 7.1 likes per 100 views. The rest of the channel averages 3.0 likes per 100 (5 likes on 167 views). No video has a comment. So Ep 16 reached more people but nobody acted on it. Ep 15 did slightly better on likes, but 3 likes is too few to read anything into.
- **Retention, traffic, countries:** YouTube Analytics came back empty for all three, so we don't know who watched, from where, or for how long.
- **What the numbers can't tell us yet:** whether views came from the Shorts feed or from people opening Ep 15 and then Ep 16 on the channel page; how much of the episode people watched; and whether 50 views is real lift or one small test batch from YouTube. Ep 16 is also the newest upload, so it has had the least time to collect views. That makes the jump more likely to be real, but not certain.

**Publish time is the clearest pattern in the data:**
- Ep 1 at 04:06 IST: 2 views.
- Ep 2–4 at midday (12:10–14:18): 20–22 views each.
- Ep 5–10, six uploads 7–8 minutes apart: 0–8 views each.
- Ep 12–14 between 00:09 and 01:43 at night: 2–12 views.
- Ep 15–16 at 07:30–07:45 on a Wednesday morning, after a 30-hour gap: 42–50 views.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is an accusation said straight to her, with a name and an object in hand: 'ये फ़ोन किसका है, रिया? झूठ मत बोलना... आज नहीं।' (Whose phone is this, Riya? Don't lie... not today.) There's no scene-setting. A viewer gets a conflict (a hidden phone), a relationship (a couple) and a stake (a lie) at once, without needing Ep 1–15. The phone buzzing a moment later adds a second jolt. Guess: this cold-open confrontation works better for new viewers than episodes that open by continuing the story.

## Psychology
- **Curiosity gap twice over:** 'कौन-सी डायरी?' (which diary?) is answered inside the episode. Then 'कल रात तुम कहाँ थे?' (where were you last night?) is left open, and the episode cuts to black on Kabir's half-lit face. That's a classic open loop that pulls people to the next episode.
- **Feeling:** first fear (he catches her lying), then relief (he says 'साथ में', together), then betrayal (now he's the suspect). The swing from relief to suspicion is what K-drama cliffhangers are built on.
- **Why no likes or comments:** the question at the end is perfect for a comment ('Kabir is hiding something'), but nobody asked for one. Ep 16 having more views than Ep 15 suggests some people watched the two back-to-back (guess).

## Topic and timing
Fake marriage with a countdown, a secret about a dead or missing mother, and a stolen diary are K-drama staples adapted for Indian homes. The title's 'साठवें दिन' (60th day) is a concrete deadline inside the 100-day contract, which gives the stakes a number. Searches found no big news or viral moment tied to this on 28 October 2026. Chhath is 13–16 November, so it doesn't explain anything. Guess, not checked: Karwa Chauth, a festival about husbands and wives, falls around the end of October 2026. That might have given a married-couple drama a small seasonal boost. With no country data we can only assume viewers were in India, judging by the publish slot and the Hindi. The jump probably happened in the morning commute window, 07:30–10:00 IST.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title packs three beats in a row: a threat, a confession, an alliance. It's specific ('साठवें दिन की धमकी', the 60th-day threat) where earlier titles were vaguer ('दादी की शर्त', grandma's condition). It still opens with 'Ep 16', which tells a stranger they've missed 15 parts (guess: this costs cold clicks). The description ends on the cliffhanger question, which is good, but doesn't ask for a comment. All episodes use the same hashtags, so hashtags didn't make the difference. We have no thumbnail data, and Shorts in the feed mostly don't show one anyway.

## Audience and algorithm
Without traffic data this part is a guess. The most likely story: YouTube gave the morning pair a fresh test batch in the Shorts feed, because nothing had been posted for 30 hours. The earlier bursts split one small batch across six videos and starved each of them. Some views probably came from the channel page or from viewers going Ep 15 to Ep 16. Search and outside links are unlikely at this size.

## What did not matter
- **Hashtags:** the same on every episode.
- **Series name and 'Ep N' format:** also the same everywhere.
- **How many uploads:** posting six episodes in an hour didn't add up to more views.
- **Plot reveals alone:** Ep 9 ('मीरा ज़िंदा है?', is Meera alive?) has an equally strong reveal and got 8 views. That points to timing and spacing, not just the story.

## Repeat this
- Post in the 07:00–08:30 or 12:00–14:30 IST windows, with hours between uploads.
- Open on an accusation with a name and an object in hand.
- Set a numbered deadline inside the 100 days.
- Explain one mystery inside the episode and open a new one at the end that points at a character the audience trusts.
- Cut to black on a face before the answer.

## Test next
- Move 'Ep N' to the end of the title and put the threat first. Compare against Ep 15–16 at the same time slot.
- Add a direct comment question to the description and the pinned comment, and see whether comments go above 0.
- Try an evening slot (19:30–21:00 IST) against morning.
- Fill in retention and traffic sources at 48 hours to confirm or drop the timing explanation.

Write the number below. Ep 17 tomorrow at 7:30 am.) Create a public playlist '100 दिन का रिश्ता — पूरी कहानी' (100-day relationship: the full story) with Ep 1–16 in order. In YouTube Studio, set each Short's related video to the next episode. Check retention and traffic sources for Ep 15 and 16 after 48 hours.

breakouts.name: Instinct
breakouts.title: SAMPLE | 235 ms pour décider : la corneille #Shorts
breakouts.summary: The crow Short didn't really break out on its own. Instinct's Shorts tend to land in one of two groups: most get under 20 views, and six of the 13 (this one included) got 477 to 1,362. It got into the larger group because it carried a precise, surprising number ('235 ms') about a corvid. It went out on 27 Oct, the day after French science sites covered the Science study on 26–27 Oct, and the like rate (4.1 per 100 views) matches the channel's other higher-view Shorts. Retention and traffic data are missing, so the exact route it took to viewers is still a guess.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **Views:** 509 against a channel median of 15.5, about 33 times higher. But that median hides a two-group channel. Six of 13 Shorts got 477–1,362 views (cigogne 1,362, corbeau 1,238, dauphin 1,191, perroquet 762, **corneille 509**, tardigrades 477). The other seven got 0–18. So this Short joined a group that already exists; it didn't create a new one.
- **Likes per 100 views:** 4.1 (21/509). The other higher-view Shorts average 3.8 (191/5,030), ranging from 2.8 for the parrot to 4.3 for the dolphin. The channel as a whole is 3.9. The low-view Shorts show about 10.6, but on roughly 47 views, which probably means the owner's own circle. So this Short was liked at a normal rate, no better.
- **Comments:** 0. The whole channel has 2 comments across 5,586 views. Nothing got people talking.
- **Can't tell yet:** YouTube Analytics came back empty: no retention, no swipe-away rate, no traffic sources, no countries. Whether it was pushed by the Shorts feed, search or France specifically is a **guess**. The two Shorts at 0 views were published just before this data was pulled, so they don't count yet.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
We don't have the script. The title, which probably shows as the opening caption, starts with a precise, odd number: '235 ms'. All six higher-view Shorts start with a concrete number or a short story setup. **Guess:** the opening line said the 235 ms out loud and compared it to humans ('twice as fast as you'). The French press framed the story exactly that way.

## Psychology
- **Feeling challenged by a bird:** 'a crow decides faster than you' prods the viewer's ego. It's a clean curiosity gap: how can a brain without a cortex do that?
- **A number you can repeat:** '235 milliseconds' is easy to quote to someone else, which helps sharing (guess: we have no share data).
- The description ends with 'Réflexe ou décision ?', but it got no comments. The question probably never appeared on screen or in the voice-over.

## Topic and timing
- The Science paper (Schmidbauer & Nieder) came out on 22 Oct 2026. French coverage followed on 26–27 Oct (Trust My Science, Consoglobe, Martin Cid FR), with English coverage (Earth.com, Science podcast) at the same time. The Short went out at 13:47 Paris time on 27 Oct, right during that French wave. People who had just seen the headline were primed to watch.
- **Birds are a pattern:** all four bird Shorts old enough to judge did well (cigogne, corbeau, corneille, perroquet). All five mammal or octopus Shorts did badly (chimp Ayumu 5, bonobo 4, elephant 7, dog 13, octopus 18). That's a small sample, but it's the cleanest split in the data.
- **Guess:** Halloween (31 Oct) gives crows a bit of extra seasonal pull.
- Countries: unknown. My guess is France, Belgium and Quebec, where the news ran.

## Title, description and thumbnail
- The title follows the house formula, 'Number : animal + action', which shows up among both the hits and the flops. So the formula is necessary but not enough on its own.
- The 'SAMPLE |' prefix and the paragraph about a fictional partnership didn't stop it. Most viewers in the Shorts feed never read titles or descriptions.
- The full source list (Science DOI, Tübingen) builds credibility, but it doesn't drive reach.

## Audience and algorithm
Most likely route (**guess**): the Shorts feed tested it with a seed batch of viewers. It cleared the bar and got a second batch, then stalled at around 500 views. The like rate is the same as the other higher-view Shorts, so all six were probably judged the same way, on retention. The flops probably failed in the first test. Search could have added a little, since people were searching 'corneille 235 millisecondes' that week, but that's unproven.

## What did not matter
- **Publish hour:** hits went out at 05:34, 10:33, 13:29 and 13:47 Paris time. Flops went out at 05:00, 12:30 and 14:41.
- **Hashtag:** the biggest Short (cigogne) has no #Shorts tag.
- **Sponsorship text and the SAMPLE label** made no visible difference.
- **Repeating a topic:** the dolphin 'name' Short hit, but the elephant version of the same idea flopped. Copying a format to a new animal doesn't carry the hit with it.

## Repeat this
1. Cover a peer-reviewed animal study within 3–7 days of its release, while French media are still running it.
2. Lead with one precise, surprising number plus a 'versus you' comparison.
3. Prefer birds, especially corvids and parrots, along with cetaceans and extreme survivors like tardigrades.
4. Keep the sources in the description.

## Test next
- Put a yes/no question on screen in the last second to break the zero-comment streak.
- Try the same bird-plus-news formula with and without the '(histoire vraie)' story framing that the stork Short used.
- Once Analytics is connected, compare retention at 3 s and 100% between the hits and the flops. That's what confirms or kills the retention guess above.

Réflexe ou vraie décision ? 👇 ». 3) Make a playlist called « Oiseaux plus malins que nous » with the corneille, corbeau, perroquet and cigogne Shorts. 4) Connect or export YouTube Analytics (retention, traffic sources, countries) so the next study can confirm the guesses in this one.

Mr. Hope: Every week, split Shorts into those above and below 300 views and record animal group, news age in days, hook number and publish hour for each, so the bird and news-timing patterns can be confirmed or dropped.

breakouts.name: Instinct
breakouts.title: 3 tardigrades ont survécu aux UV en orbite #Shorts
breakouts.summary: The tardigrade Short got 477 views, about 31 times the channel's usual 16, but it is not a one-off. Six of the channel's 13 recent Shorts have passed YouTube's first Shorts-feed test, and this was one of the smaller hits (the crow, dolphin and stork Shorts each got over 1,100 views). It got through because it took a famous 'indestructible' animal and opened with a fact that breaks that myth (it survived space, but the sun's UV nearly killed it), and it ended on an open question that brought in the only comment of the week.
breakouts.report:
## The numbers
- **477 views against a usual 15.5, about 31 times more.** But 'usual' here is a median that hides a two-camp channel. Six Shorts got 477 to 1,362 views (stork 1,362, crow wire 1,238, dolphin 1,191, parrot 762, crow 235 ms 509, tardigrade 477). Seven got 0 to 18. The tardigrade is the **smallest of the hits**, so the real question is what the hits share.
- **Likes per 100 views: 3.98** against 3.88 for the rest of the channel (198 likes on 5,109 views). That is normal for a hit here (dolphin 4.28, crow 4.04, stork 3.67, parrot 2.76).
- **Comments: 1, which is 0.21 per 100 views**, against 0.02 for the rest of the channel (1 comment on 5,109 views). That is about 10 times the rate, but it is a single comment.
- **Retention, traffic sources and countries: empty.** We can't yet tell what share watched to the end, whether views came from the Shorts feed or from search, or which countries watched. The 0-view bee and 47-crows Shorts, and the 4-view bonobo, went out less than a day before this data was pulled, so they don't count as flops yet.

## Hook and first 2 seconds
The first line is « Ils ont survécu au vide de l'espace. Les UV du soleil, eux, en ont presque eu raison. » Sentence one gives the myth everyone already knows. Sentence two breaks it straight away. On screen, a macro shot of a tardigrade with « Vide ✅ UV complets ⚠️ » shows the twist before the voice has finished it. The losing Shorts mostly open on a plain fact (octopus: 3 hearts) or a name nobody knows (Ayumu), with no twist.

## Psychology
- **Watch:** a curiosity gap built on a known myth. Most people have heard that tardigrades are 'indestructible', so « presque eu raison » makes them want to know what nearly beat it.
- **Finish:** the numbers come in steps (10 days, 270 km, 3 survivors, 7,000 kJ/m²), and the big « 3 survivants » card at 0:42 pays off what the title promised. *Guess:* that card held people to the end.
- **Comment:** the ending leaves the question open (« La question reste ouverte ») and then asks for a one-word answer. A low-effort ask after an unsolved puzzle is the best-known trigger for comments. This was the only Short with that structure, and it got the comment.
- **Share/like:** a small animal beating space, plus a scientist-style 'nobody knows yet', is the kind of thing you send to someone. *Guess*, since we have no share data.

## Topic and timing
Tardigrades are one of the internet's evergreen stars, popular because they seem almost indestructible. October 2026 also had tardigrade stories in the news: the ACS press release on tardigrade proteins protecting frozen blood (8 Oct), and French regional press around 11 Oct on Montpellier researchers « percent les secrets du tardigrade ». So French readers had recently seen « survit au vide spatial » headlines. Nothing happened on 27 October itself, no news and no holiday, so the ambient interest probably helped and a same-day trigger didn't (*guess*). It was published at 10:04 IST, which is **05:34 Paris**, 04:34 Dakar/Abidjan and 00:34 Montreal. That is not the 15:00 or 21:00 Paris slot the script planned. We can't see countries yet.

## Title, description and thumbnail
The title « 3 tardigrades ont survécu aux UV en orbite » has a number, a famous animal named plainly, a past-tense result and an unusual setting. Every hit except the 235 ms crow follows that pattern: « répond », « plie », « dit aucun », « vole 13 000 km ». Among the losers, Ayumu is a name viewers don't know and the title has no verb. The elephant title ends in a question mark and copies the dolphin title from the day before. The octopus title states a mild preference. *Guess:* a clear, surprising result in the title matters. The description (sources, Paris-Caen comparison) builds trust but is barely seen in the feed.

## Audience and algorithm
With no traffic data, the pattern points to the **Shorts feed**. Hits on this channel land between 500 and 1,400 views, and losers stall under 20. That looks like YouTube testing each Short on a small group of viewers and only pushing it wider if they stop scrolling and keep watching. Search may add a little, because « tardigrade » is a searched word, but it wouldn't produce this jump-or-nothing pattern. There is no sign of outside traffic.

## What did not matter
- **Publish time:** the parrot at 05:30 Paris got 762 views, and the dog at 05:00 Paris got 13.
- **Starting the title with a number:** every Short does it, hits and losers alike.
- **Hashtags, the thumbnail plan and the length (~57 s):** the same on all of them.
- **Narrator-only vs story:** both formats appear among the hits and the losers.

## Repeat this
1. A famous animal plus a twist that breaks its myth, inside the first 2 seconds, in voice and on-screen text together.
2. Numbers that build towards one big card showing the payoff.
3. End on a real open question and ask for a one-word answer.
4. Title pattern: number + common animal name + past-tense result + unusual setting.

## Test next
- A tardigrade follow-up that answers « qu'est-ce qui les protège ? » (Dsup and other protective proteins, the October 2026 blood-freezing study), to see whether the open-question ending builds a series.
- A question-mark title against a statement title on the same type of topic.
- A twist hook against a plain-fact hook on two famous animals the same week.
- One more true story with a human and an animal, like the stork (1,362 views, the top Short).

Mr. Pen: Write the first two sentences as myth then twist, both inside 3 seconds (e.g. « Ils ont survécu au vide. Les UV, eux, ont failed de les tuer. » style). End every script with the question the study leaves open, followed by « Un mot en commentaire ».
